title: ¿Cuándo debo empezar terapia física después de un accidente de auto?
d: Una vez que un médico haya descartado una lesión grave, como una fractura, empezar pronto con movimiento y ejercicio guiados es generalmente mejor que esperar a que el dolor se quite solo.

title: ¿Debo usar un collarín?
d: Para el latigazo cervical sin fractura, las guías generalmente no recomiendan un collarín blando. El movimiento suave ayuda más a la recuperación que mantener el cuello quieto.

title: ¿Por qué el dolor empezó uno o dos días después del accidente?
d: Es común. Los músculos y las articulaciones lastimados a menudo se ponen rígidos y duelen más durante las primeras 24 a 48 horas.

title: ¿Necesito una referencia médica después de un accidente de auto?
d: En California puede ver a un fisioterapeuta directamente hasta por 12 visitas o 45 días. Algunos seguros, incluidos los reclamos al seguro de auto, pueden pedir una referencia del médico para cubrir el tratamiento, así que llámenos y le ayudamos a verificarlo.

title: ¿El latigazo cervical puede causar dolores de cabeza?
d: Sí. Los dolores de cabeza en la base del cráneo son uno de los síntomas más comunes después de un latigazo cervical, y tratar el cuello a menudo ayuda a aliviarlos.

title: Why Is My Achilles Tendon Stiff and Sore in the Morning?
d: Morning stiffness in the Achilles tendon is a classic sign of Achilles tendinopathy. Why it happens, why rest alone rarely fixes it, and what helps.

x: Patient Questions / Achilles pain in the morning Foot & Ankle Why Is My Achilles Tendon Stiff and Sore in the Morning? Morning stiffness that eases once you get moving is a classic sign of Achilles tendinopathy, an overload problem in the tendon at the back of your heel. It usually comes from doing more than the tendon is ready for. It's common, and strengthening exercise is the main treatment. Request an Evaluation Why mornings are worst Overnight, your tendon rests in a shortened position and stiffens up. The first steps out of bed load it before it has warmed up. Many people find it loosens after a few minutes of walking, then feels sore again later in the day or the next morning after a lot of activity. Common causes include a sudden increase in running or walking, more hills or stairs, a change in shoes, tight or weak calf muscles, and age. It’s common in runners and in middle-aged people who are on their feet a lot. What helps Calf strengthening , such as heel raises, built up gradually. Loading exercise has the strongest evidence for Achilles tendinopathy. Adjust, don’t stop. Cut back on what flares it, like hills or speed work. Complete rest usually doesn’t fix tendon pain. Use the next morning as your guide. If stiffness is much worse the day after an activity, it was too much. Gently move your ankle before you get out of bed. title: Do all ACL tears need surgery?
d: No. Many active people choose ACL reconstruction, especially for sports with pivoting and cutting. Some people do well with rehab alone, particularly if they don't play pivoting sports. Your surgeon and physical therapist can help you decide.

title: How long is recovery after ACL reconstruction?
d: Most people walk normally within a few weeks and return to running after a few months. Return to pivoting sports usually takes at least about nine months, once strength and movement tests show the knee is ready.

title: Does an MCL tear need surgery?
d: Usually not. Most MCL sprains heal with a period of protection, often a brace, and a progressive rehab program.

title: Can physical therapy help before ACL surgery?
d: Yes. Getting swelling down, restoring full motion and building strength before reconstruction is linked with a smoother recovery afterward.

title: Do I need a doctor's referral for physical therapy in California?
d: No. In California you can see a physical therapist directly for up to 12 visits or 45 days, whichever comes first. Some insurance plans still require a referral for coverage, so call us at (661) 282-8584 and we'll help you check.

For women, common causes include a urinary tract infection, an overactive bladder, drinks that irritate the bladder, a habit of going "just in case," and pelvic floor muscles that are tight or weak. Your doctor should check for infection first. Request an Evaluation Common causes Urinary tract infection (UTI). Often comes with burning, but not always. A simple urine test can check. Overactive bladder. The bladder sends strong “go now” signals before it's full. Bladder irritants like coffee, tea, soda, alcohol and artificial sweeteners. Habits. Other factors such as constipation, menopause changes, prolapse, pregnancy, some medicines, or bladder pain conditions. What helps For overactive bladder, treatment guidelines recommend starting with behavior changes and pelvic floor training before or alongside medicine: Bladder training: slowly stretching the time between bathroom trips. title: Should I rest a sprained ankle completely?
d: Usually not for long. After the first few days, gentle movement and walking as pain allows help a sprain heal. A physical therapist can guide you on when to add balance and strengthening work.

title: Why does my ankle keep rolling?
d: After a sprain, the ankle's strength and balance reactions often don't fully recover on their own, which makes another sprain more likely. Balance and strength training can reduce that risk.

title: Should I stop running with Achilles pain?
d: Not always. Many people can keep some running or walking while the tendon gets stronger, as long as pain stays mild and settles by the next day. Your therapist will help you adjust your training.

title: How long does Achilles tendon pain take to get better?
d: Tendons improve slowly. Many people notice progress within several weeks of consistent loading exercise, with full recovery taking a few months. Sticking with the program is what makes the difference.

Medical guidelines recommend staying as active as you comfortably can, because bed rest tends to slow recovery. Medical guidelines advise against routine imaging for new back pain unless there are warning signs, because most back pain improves with time and active treatment, and scans often show changes that aren't causing the pain. x: Patient Questions / Shoes for heel pain Foot & Ankle What Kind of Shoes Help Heel Pain? Shoes with good arch support, a cushioned heel and a slightly raised heel usually feel best for heel pain, and going barefoot on hard floors often makes it worse. Shoes help, but stretching and strengthening are what fix it. Request an Evaluation What to look for A cushioned, slightly raised heel. A small heel-to-toe drop takes some strain off the plantar fascia and calf. Arch support. Firm midsoles and supportive insoles help many people. Over-the-counter inserts are often enough. A stable sole that doesn't twist easily. Fresh cushioning. Worn-out shoes lose support. Replace walking or running shoes regularly. title: Can Working at a Desk Cause Neck Pain and Headaches?

x: Patient Questions / Desk work, neck pain and headaches Neck, Jaw & Headaches Can Working at a Desk Cause Neck Pain and Headaches? Yes. Long hours at a screen can tire and stiffen the neck and upper back, and some headaches actually start in the neck. Movement breaks, a better setup and targeted strengthening often help. Request an Evaluation How desk work affects your neck When you work at a computer or phone for long stretches, your head tends to drift forward and your shoulders round. Holding that position for hours keeps the neck and upper-back muscles working without a break. Over time they get tired and sore, and the joints get stiff. Some headaches, called cervicogenic headaches , come from the neck. They often start at the base of the skull or on one side, can spread to the forehead or behind the eye, and get worse with certain neck positions or long hours at a desk. Simple changes that help Put the top of your screen near eye level, about an arm's length away. Keep your keyboard and mouse close so your elbows stay by your sides. Get up and move every 30 to 45 minutes, even for a minute. Hold your phone higher instead of looking down at it for long periods. Strengthen the muscles that support your neck and shoulder blades. title: What is the difference between a bulging disc and a herniated disc?
d: A bulging disc spreads out a little past its normal edge. It is very common and often causes no pain. A herniated disc means some of the soft center has pushed through the outer ring, and it is more likely to irritate a nerve. Both often improve with exercise and time.

title: Can a herniated disc heal on its own?
d: Often, yes. Many herniated discs shrink over weeks to months as the body reabsorbs part of the disc material, and most people improve without surgery. Staying active and doing the right exercises usually helps you feel better while that happens.

title: Should I avoid sitting with a herniated disc?
d: You don't have to avoid it, but long stretches of sitting often make disc pain worse. Getting up every 30 to 45 minutes, a small cushion or rolled towel behind your low back, and short walks during the day can help. Your therapist can suggest what works for your symptoms.

title: Can I still lift things with a herniated disc?
d: Usually yes, with a plan. Heavy lifting, especially while bending and twisting, may need to wait while your symptoms are flared up, but avoiding lifting for good tends to leave the back weaker. We build lifting back up step by step, starting light.

title: Will I need surgery for my disc?
d: Most people do not. Surgery is usually considered for severe or worsening weakness, warning signs like bladder or bowel changes, or leg pain that doesn't improve with good conservative care. If you do have surgery, rehab afterward helps you recover.

Lying on that side presses on them. Lying on the other side can hurt too, because your top leg drops across your body and stretches them. Other common triggers include standing with your weight on one hip, crossing your legs, climbing stairs, and a sudden jump in walking or running. Changes in hormones around menopause may make these tendons more sensitive, which is one reason it’s more common in women. title: How long does a pinched nerve in the neck take to get better?
d: It varies. Many people improve over several weeks to a few months, and the arm pain often eases before numbness or tingling does. If your symptoms are getting worse instead of better, or weakness is increasing, see your doctor.

title: Is it a pinched nerve or carpal tunnel?
d: Both can cause numbness and tingling in the hand. A pinched nerve in the neck often comes with neck or shoulder blade pain, and symptoms that change with neck movement. title: What is the best sleeping position for a pinched nerve in the neck?
d: Most people do best on their back or side, with a pillow that keeps the head level, not propped up or dropping down. Stomach sleeping keeps the neck turned for hours and often makes symptoms worse. Some people find resting the sore arm on a pillow helps.

x: Patient Questions / Room spins when rolling over Dizziness & Balance Why Does the Room Spin When I Roll Over in Bed? Brief spinning, lasting less than a minute, when you roll over, lie down or look up is usually BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo). Tiny crystals in the inner ear move out of place. It's very treatable, often in just a few visits. Request an Evaluation What BPPV is Your inner ear contains tiny calcium crystals that help sense movement. Sometimes, after a head bump, an illness, or for no clear reason, especially as we get older, some crystals drift into one of the balance canals. Then certain head movements trigger a burst of spinning. Typical signs: spinning that starts a few seconds after rolling over, lying down, getting up, or tipping your head back, and stops within a minute. Some people feel off-balance or queasy for a while afterward. How it's treated BPPV is treated with repositioning maneuvers , such as the Epley maneuver: a series of head and body positions that guide the crystals back where they belong. Clinical guidelines recommend these maneuvers, and many people feel better within one to a few visits. Medication for dizziness doesn't fix BPPV. Because there are different types of BPPV, a trained physical therapist first tests which ear and canal is involved. Aching around or behind the kneecap with squatting, running, stairs or long sitting is usually patellofemoral pain, often called runner's knee. It's treated well with hip and thigh strengthening and adjusting your training load. Request an Evaluation What is runner's knee? Patellofemoral pain is irritation where the kneecap glides over the thigh bone. You don't have to be a runner to get it: it's common in teens, active adults and people who have recently increased walking, hiking, squatting or stairs. Typical signs are a dull ache around the kneecap that is worse with squatting, stairs, kneeling, running downhill, or sitting with your knees bent for a long time (the “movie-goer's sign”). Why it happens It usually comes from doing more than the knee is ready for , for example a jump in running mileage, combined with thigh and hip muscles that aren't strong enough to control the knee. The knee often drifts inward during squats and landing. What helps Strengthening the hip and thigh muscles is the treatment with the strongest research support. Cut back, but don't stop: reduce mileage or depth of squats to a level that doesn't flare it, then build back up gradually. title: How do I know if my pain is from the SI joint or my back?
d: It can be hard to tell. SI joint pain is usually on one side, near the dimple at the back of the pelvis, and it often hurts with stairs, standing on one leg or rolling over in bed. Pain that runs below the knee, or tingling in the foot, is more likely to come from the low back. A physical therapy evaluation uses a group of tests to sort it out.

title: Can my SI joint go out of place?
d: Rarely. The SI joints are strong, tightly braced joints that move only a small amount. The pain usually comes from irritation of the joint and the tissues around it, and strengthening and hands-on treatment can help.

title: Is SI joint pain common in pregnancy?
d: Yes. Pain at the back of the pelvis is very common during pregnancy, as hormones loosen the ligaments and your posture changes. For many women it improves after birth, and gentle physical therapy can help both during pregnancy and afterward.

title: Should I wear an SI belt?
d: A support belt helps some people, especially during pregnancy or for walking and standing tasks. It works best as a short-term aid alongside strengthening, not as the whole treatment. Your therapist can tell you whether one is likely to help you.

title: What is the best sleeping position for SI joint pain?
d: Many people are most comfortable on their side with a pillow between the knees, or on their back with a pillow under the knees. When you roll over, keep your knees together and turn your body as one unit.

title: Will spinal stenosis get worse over time?
d: Not always. Stenosis tends to change slowly, and for many people symptoms stay about the same or improve with exercise rather than steadily getting worse. Your therapist and doctor can help you watch for changes that need attention.

title: Is walking good for spinal stenosis?
d: Yes, in the right amounts. Short, frequent walks with planned rest breaks often work better than one long walk. Leaning slightly forward, using a cart or walker on longer outings, and building up gradually can help you go farther.

title: What should I avoid with spinal stenosis?
d: Positions that keep your back arched for a long time, like standing still for long periods or reaching overhead, often bring on leg symptoms. You don't have to avoid them for good, but it helps to break them up. Your therapist will show you which exercises ease your symptoms.

title: Do I need surgery for spinal stenosis?
d: Many people manage well without surgery. Surgery, such as a laminectomy, may be considered if symptoms are severe, keep getting worse, or don't improve with good treatment. That is a decision to make with your doctor, and rehab helps either way.

No. Many meniscus tears, especially wear-related tears in people over about 40, improve with exercise therapy. Studies found that for these tears, exercise can work as well as arthroscopic surgery. Request an Evaluation Two kinds of meniscus tears The meniscus is the cartilage cushion between the thigh and shin bones. Wear-related (degenerative) tears happen gradually with age. They are very common on MRI, even in people with no knee pain at all. Injury-related tears happen with a twist, often in sport, and are more common in younger people. What the research shows For middle-aged and older adults with a wear-related tear, several well-designed studies found that a supervised exercise program gave similar results to arthroscopic surgery for pain and function. That's why many orthopedic surgeons now recommend trying physical therapy first. When surgery may be the better choice A surgeon may recommend surgery if your knee truly locks and won't straighten, if a torn piece is caught in the joint, or for some injury-related tears in younger, active people where repairing the meniscus is possible. It's usually very treatable with physical therapy, often in just a few visits. Request an Evaluation Yes, physical therapy can treat vertigo caused by BPPV. BPPV happens when tiny calcium crystals in the inner ear drift into the wrong place, so certain head movements set off a brief, intense spinning feeling. El VPPB (vértigo posicional paroxístico benigno) ocurre cuando unos pequeños cristales de calcio del oído interno se mueven al lugar equivocado, y entonces ciertos movimientos de la cabeza provocan una sensación breve e intensa de que todo da vueltas. La guía de práctica clínica de la American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery recomienda maniobras de reposicionamiento, como la maniobra de Epley, para regresar los cristales a su lugar. Un fisioterapeuta capacitado puede identificar qué oído y qué conducto están afectados y tratarlo, y muchas personas se sienten mucho mejor en una a tres sesiones. ¿Le suena familiar? ✓ El cuarto le da vueltas cuando se voltea en la cama o se acuesta ✓ Mirar hacia una repisa alta o echar la cabeza hacia atrás lo provoca ✓ Agacharse o levantarse de la cama le marea ✓ Las vueltas duran segundos, por lo general menos de un minuto ✓ Siente náuseas o se siente inestable por un r

title: ¿De verdad un fisioterapeuta puede quitar el vértigo?
d: Para el VPPB, a menudo sí. El VPPB se debe a cristales del oído interno fuera de lugar, y las maniobras de reposicionamiento que hace un fisioterapeuta capacitado los regresan a su lugar. Muchas personas se sienten mucho mejor en una a tres sesiones.

title: ¿Es lo mismo que la maniobra de Epley que vi en internet?
d: La maniobra de Epley es uno de los tratamientos de reposicionamiento. Solo funciona para el VPPB en un conducto en particular, del lado correcto. Una evaluación identifica qué oído y qué conducto están afectados, para usar la maniobra correcta.

title: ¿El tratamiento me va a marear?
d: Puede ser, por un momento. Las pruebas y la maniobra pueden provocar las vueltas por unos segundos, y eso es de esperarse. Su fisioterapeuta se queda con usted y va a su ritmo.

title: ¿El vértigo puede regresar?
d: El VPPB puede regresar, a veces meses o años después. La buena noticia es que por lo general responde de nuevo al mismo tratamiento, y su fisioterapeuta puede enseñarle qué señales vigilar.

title: What Does a Pinched Nerve Feel Like?

x: Patient Questions / What a pinched nerve feels like Neck, Jaw & Headaches What Does a Pinched Nerve Feel Like? A pinched nerve often causes sharp, burning or electric pain that travels along a line, such as from the neck down the arm or from the low back down the leg. It may come with tingling, pins and needles, numbness or weakness. Muscle pain, by contrast, is usually achy and stays in one area. Most pinched nerves improve without surgery. Request an Evaluation Common signs of a pinched nerve Pain that travels into the shoulder blade, arm or hand (from the neck), or into the buttock, leg or foot (from the low back). Sharp, shooting, burning or electric pain, rather than a dull ache. Tingling, pins and needles or numbness in part of the arm, hand, leg or foot. Weakness , like a weaker grip or a foot that drags. Certain positions make it worse , such as looking up or turning your head toward the sore side. Some people with a pinched neck nerve find that resting their hand on top of their head eases the arm pain. The medical name is radiculopathy . It usually happens when a disc bulge or narrowing near the spine irritates a nerve root. Nerve pain or muscle pain? Muscle pain tends to be achy, sore to touch and limited to one area. title: What Is the Epley Maneuver, and Can I Do It at Home?

x: Patient Questions / The Epley maneuver Dizziness & Balance What Is the Epley Maneuver, and Can I Do It at Home? The Epley maneuver is a series of head and body positions that moves loose inner-ear crystals back where they belong. It treats the most common type of BPPV, which causes brief spinning when you move your head. Some people can do it at home, but it's best to have BPPV confirmed first and learn it from a trained clinician. Request an Evaluation How it works In BPPV, tiny calcium crystals drift into one of the inner ear’s balance canals. The Epley maneuver moves your head through a set sequence, holding each position for a short time, so gravity rolls the crystals out of the canal. It may bring on a brief burst of spinning while it works. Clinical guidelines recommend repositioning maneuvers like the Epley for BPPV, and many people feel better after one to a few treatments. Doing it at home Home versions can help, especially if BPPV comes back after it’s been confirmed. But there are good reasons to get checked first: Right side, right canal. The Epley is done differently for the left and right ear, and it doesn’t work for every type of BPPV. Other types need other maneuvers. Not all dizziness is BPPV. Practice getting in and out of the passenger seat: back up to the seat, sit down, then swing your legs in together. Get care quickly if a joint is hot, red and swollen, especially with fever, if you can't use it or put weight on it after an injury, or if it looks out of place. It feels stiff at first, then loosens up as you move. It is in one or two joints and has been slowly changing over time. You feel well otherwise, with no fever or weight loss. This kind of pain is common, and it is often helped by exercise, staying active and pacing. It's still worth getting checked if it isn't improving after a few weeks or is stopping you from doing things you care about. Signs to see a doctor soon Several joints swollen at once , especially the small joints of the hands or feet, with morning stiffness that lasts more than an hour. This can be inflammatory arthritis, like rheumatoid arthritis, which does best with early treatment. Sudden, very painful swelling in one joint, like the big toe, which can be gout. Standing still keeps the same muscles working and your low back slightly arched for a long time, so the joints and muscles can get tired and achy. It's common in people who stand at work. If the pain spreads into your buttocks or legs and eases when you sit or lean forward, it may be spinal stenosis, especially after age 50. When you stand still, the same muscles hold you up the whole time and the small joints at the back of the spine stay under steady pressure. title: Why Does My Jaw Click or Pop When I Open My Mouth?
d: Jaw clicking is common and often harmless when there is no pain. What causes it, simple habits that help, and when a clicking jaw is worth getting checked.
h: What's happening inside the joint · Simple things that may help · When to see a doctor · How physical therapy at ARI can help · Related questions
x: Patient Questions / Jaw clicking or popping Neck, Jaw & Headaches Why Does My Jaw Click or Pop When I Open My Mouth? Usually because the small cushion (disc) inside your jaw joint shifts slightly as you open and close. Jaw clicking is very common, and if it doesn't hurt and your jaw moves normally, it's often nothing to worry about. Pain, locking or trouble opening your mouth are reasons to get it checked. Request an Evaluation What's happening inside the joint Your jaw joint, called the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) , sits just in front of each ear. A small disc sits between the bones and moves as you open your mouth. If the disc slips a little out of place, it can click or pop as it slides back. Muscle tension and how the two sides of the jaw move together can also play a part. Many people have a clicking jaw for years without any problems. It becomes more of a concern when it comes with pain, headaches, or your jaw catching or getting stuck. title: Why Does My Jaw Click or Pop When I Open My Mouth?

title: Why Does My Knee Hurt When I Kneel?

x: Patient Questions / Knee pain when kneeling Knee Why Does My Knee Hurt When I Kneel? Kneeling puts direct pressure on your kneecap and the tissues in front of it. Common causes of pain are an irritated bursa in front of the kneecap, kneecap pain, knee arthritis, or a sore tendon just below the kneecap. title: Why Does My Knee Swell After Exercise?

x: Patient Questions / Knee swelling after exercise Knee Why Does My Knee Swell After Exercise? Common causes include a strained muscle, a sensitive disc or stiff joints. Your spine is built to bend, and most bending pain gets better as you keep moving and slowly get used to bending again. title: Why Does My Neck Crack and Pop, and Is It Bad?
d: Neck cracking and popping is usually harmless. What causes the sound, when it's worth getting checked, and why forceful self-cracking isn't a good habit.

x: Patient Questions / Neck cracking and popping Neck, Jaw & Headaches Why Does My Neck Crack and Pop, and Is It Bad? Usually it's harmless. The sound is most often a small gas bubble releasing in a joint, or a tendon sliding over bone. Painless cracking is common and isn't known to cause arthritis. It's worth getting checked if it comes with pain, numbness or dizziness, or if you feel you need to crack it all the time. Request an Evaluation What makes the sound Gas bubbles. The joints in your neck are surrounded by fluid. When a joint is stretched or twisted, a bubble can form or release with a pop. That's why you often can't crack the same joint again right away. Tendons and ligaments can snap lightly over bone as you move. Grinding or crunching sounds are common with age as joint surfaces change. They are often painless and not a sign of damage on their own. Noises by themselves aren't a good guide to what's happening inside your neck. How your neck feels and moves matters much more than whether it makes sounds. Is cracking your own neck bad? An occasional gentle pop when you stretch or turn your head is fine. Forcefully twisting your neck to make it crack is different. The relief usually lasts only a short time, and in rare cases forceful neck twisting has been linked to injury of an artery in the neck. Common reasons are going back to full activity before your body is ready, the original cause not changing, like weakness or a heavy workload, and a nervous system that stays sensitive after pain. Weak hips with knee pain, or a long day in one position with back pain. A sensitive system. title: Why Does My Shoulder Click or Pop?
d: Shoulder clicking without pain is common and usually harmless. When clicking with pain, catching or weakness may point to a problem worth getting checked.

x: Patient Questions / Shoulder clicking or popping Shoulder, Elbow & Hand Why Does My Shoulder Click or Pop? Clicking or popping with no pain is very common and usually harmless. It can come from tendons sliding over bone or small gas bubbles in the joint. Clicking that comes with pain, catching, weakness or a feeling that the shoulder might slip out is worth getting checked. Request an Evaluation Harmless clicking The shoulder is a very mobile joint, with many muscles and tendons moving over bones. As you lift or rotate your arm, these soft tissues can snap or rub over each other and make noise. Some people also hear a pop that comes from gas bubbles inside the joint. If it doesn't hurt and your shoulder works well, there is usually no need to worry or to avoid the movement. Shoulder noise also tends to be more common as we age, and it can come and go. Keeping the shoulder strong and moving is good for it either way. When clicking may mean something more Rotator cuff irritation can cause a painful catch partway through lifting your arm. A labrum tear (the rim of cartilage around the socket) can cause clicking, catching or a deep ache, often after an injury or repeated overhead activity. title: Why Does My Upper Arm Hurt Near My Shoulder?

x: Patient Questions / Upper arm pain near the shoulder Shoulder, Elbow & Hand Why Does My Upper Arm Hurt Near My Shoulder? Pain on the outside of the upper arm, partway between the shoulder and elbow, very often comes from the shoulder itself. Irritated rotator cuff tendons or bursa usually send pain to that spot. It's often worse when lifting your arm, reaching behind you or lying on that side. A pinched nerve in the neck can also cause arm pain, usually with tingling. Request an Evaluation Why shoulder pain shows up in the arm The rotator cuff is a group of muscles and tendons that hold the ball of the shoulder in its socket. When those tendons or the bursa next to them are irritated, the pain is often felt lower down, in the outer upper arm , rather than in the shoulder joint. That's why many people rub their arm when the problem is really in the shoulder. Other possible causes Biceps tendon irritation , felt at the front of the shoulder and upper arm, often with lifting. A pinched nerve in the neck , which often comes with neck pain and pain, tingling or numbness that goes below the elbow. A muscle strain after a new activity, like painting a ceiling or a new workout. Frozen shoulder , where the shoulder becomes painful and steadily stiffer. title: Why Does the Back of My Knee Hurt?

Hamstring or calf tendon irritation , often after running, hills, sprinting or a jump in activity. A meniscus tear. The meniscus is a cushion inside the knee. Tears near the back can hurt with deep squatting or twisting, sometimes with catching. Knee arthritis , which can cause stiffness and ache at the back of the knee. What usually helps Calm the knee. title: Why Does the Ball of My Foot Hurt?
d: Pain in the ball of the foot is often metatarsalgia, an overloaded forefoot. Causes like shoes and Morton's neuroma, what helps, and when to get checked.
h: Common causes · What usually helps · When to see a doctor · How physical therapy at ARI can help · Related questions
x: Patient Questions / Pain in the ball of the foot Foot & Ankle Why Does the Ball of My Foot Hurt? Often it's metatarsalgia, which means the area under the bones at the base of your toes is overloaded and sore. Common causes include high heels, thin-soled shoes, lots of running or jumping, bunions or hammertoes, and the fat pad under the foot thinning with age. Burning or tingling between the toes may be a Morton's neuroma. Request an Evaluation Common causes Metatarsalgia. An aching or bruised feeling under the ball of the foot, worse when standing, walking barefoot on hard floors or wearing heels. Morton's neuroma. An irritated nerve between the toes, usually the third and fourth. It can feel like burning, tingling or standing on a pebble. A stress fracture in one of the long foot bones, often after a jump in walking, running or training. Toe joint irritation , often with bunions, hammertoes or arthritis in the big toe. What usually helps Shoes: a cushioned sole, a wide toe box and a lower heel. Some people find a stiffer “rocker” sole helps. Padding: a metatarsal pad placed just behind the sore spot can take pressure off it. Load: cut back on running, jumping or long periods on your feet for a while, then build back up gradually. Strength and flexibility: tight calves can push more load onto the front of the foot, so calf stretching and foot and calf strengthening often help.

Request an Evaluation Why a brace helps Carpal tunnel syndrome happens when the median nerve is squeezed as it passes through a narrow space in the wrist. A brace holds the wrist in a straight, neutral position , so the nerve gets a break for hours at a time. How to wear it Pick a brace that keeps the wrist straight. title: Is my child's knee pain just growing pains?
d: Not always. Growing pains usually affect both legs, come on in the evening or at night and are gone by morning. Pain in one spot, pain with sport, swelling or limping is more likely a specific problem like Osgood-Schlatter and is worth having checked.

title: Does my child have to stop playing?
d: Often not completely. Many overuse problems in young athletes do well with less load for a while, not full rest. Your therapist will help set limits that let your child stay active while the area settles.

title: Can ACL injuries be prevented?
d: The risk can be lowered. Warm-up programs that train strength, balance, landing and cutting have been shown to reduce ACL injuries in young athletes, especially girls. Your therapist can teach exercises that fit your child's sport.

title: Is it OK for my child to play one sport all year?
d: Playing one sport year-round with little rest is linked to more overuse injuries and burnout. Many sports medicine groups recommend regular rest days each week, a break from the main sport for part of the year, and trying other sports, especially for younger athletes.

title: Sciatica and back pain
d: Pain that runs from your low back into your buttock or leg, often from an irritated disc or nerve, or stiffness and aching in the back itself. Most people improve without surgery, and specific exercise and hands-on care are the recommended first step.

title: Herniated and bulging discs
d: An MRI report that says “disc bulge” or “herniation,” a back that seizes up when you bend, or pain that shoots into your leg when you sit. Disc problems sound scary, but most get better without surgery, and the right exercise is a big part of that.

title: Spinal stenosis
d: Your legs ache, tingle or feel heavy after a few minutes of walking or standing, and the only fix is to sit down or lean on something. That pattern is often lumbar spinal stenosis, and the right exercise can help you walk farther.

title: SI joint pain
d: A deep ache on one side of your low back or buttock, right around the dimple, that flares when you climb stairs, roll over in bed or stand on one leg. That pattern often points to the sacroiliac joint.

title: Headaches that start in the neck
d: Headaches that begin at the base of the skull or on one side of the head, often worse with certain neck positions or long hours at a desk. Hands-on treatment for the neck and targeted strengthening can reduce how often they come and how bad they get. A sudden, severe or “worst ever” headache needs a doctor right away.

title: Pinched nerve in the neck
d: Pain that runs from your neck into your shoulder blade and down your arm, or tingling and numbness in your fingers. A pinched nerve in the neck can be very painful, but most people get better without surgery.

title: Upper back pain and posture
d: A knot between your shoulder blades after a day at the computer, a stiff mid back when you twist, or an ache that builds while you look down at your phone. Upper back pain is common, and it usually responds well to movement, strength and a few changes to your day.

title: Neck pain and whiplash after a car accident
d: Neck pain, stiffness and headaches after a car accident can show up hours or days later. Once a doctor has ruled out a serious injury, gentle movement, hands-on care and progressive exercise help you recover and get back to normal activity. If you have severe neck pain, numbness or weakness after a crash, get checked by a doctor first.

title: Fibromyalgia and widespread pain
d: Pain in many places, fatigue and poor sleep, with good days and bad days. Gentle exercise that builds at your pace is one of the most recommended treatments for fibromyalgia, alongside your doctor's care.

title: Frozen shoulder and rotator cuff pain
d: Pain reaching overhead or behind your back, pain lying on that side at night, or a shoulder that has slowly stiffened. Physical therapy restores motion first, then rebuilds strength, and most rotator cuff and frozen shoulder problems improve without surgery.

title: Shoulder impingement and bursitis
d: A catch of pain partway up as you lift your arm, or an ache on the outside of the shoulder after reaching, lifting or overhead work. This kind of shoulder pain is very common, and most people improve with the right exercise, without surgery.

title: Tennis elbow and golfer’s elbow
d: Pain on the outside (tennis) or inside (golfer’s) of the elbow, worse with gripping, lifting or typing, and you don't have to play either sport to get it. Progressive tendon-strengthening exercise, changes to how you grip and work, and hands-on care are the mainstays of treatment.

title: Carpal tunnel and hand numbness
d: Numbness or tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, often worse at night, driving or typing. For mild to moderate symptoms, physical therapy with nerve and tendon gliding exercises, splinting advice and changes to how you use your hands can help. Constant numbness or hand weakness should be checked by a doctor.

title: Hand and wrist pain
d: A finger that catches or locks, an ache at the base of your thumb, a wrist that is stiff and weak after a cast. Your hands do almost everything, and many hand and wrist problems improve with the right exercise and a few simple changes.

title: Tendonitis and overuse injuries
d: Pain that builds with repeated gripping, lifting, running or overhead work. A progressive strengthening program is the first-line treatment for most tendon pain, with better long-term results than rest alone.

title: Hip pain and hip arthritis
d: Groin pain when you walk, stiffness putting on socks, or an aching outer hip that's worse lying on that side at night. Strengthening the hip and thigh muscles is a strongly recommended treatment for hip arthritis and painful outer-hip tendons.

title: Knee arthritis and knee pain
d: Pain on stairs, stiffness after sitting, or a knee that swells after a busy day. Exercise-based physical therapy is one of the most strongly recommended treatments for knee osteoarthritis, and for some people it can put off the need for surgery.

title: Osteoarthritis and joint pain
d: Stiff fingers in the morning, knees that complain on the stairs, a back or hip that aches after a long day. Arthritis is common as we get older, but it doesn't have to mean giving up the things you enjoy.

title: ACL and MCL knee ligament injuries
d: A twist or pop, then swelling or a knee that gives way. Most MCL sprains heal without surgery, and rehab is central to ACL recovery, with or without reconstruction, and to a safe return to sport.

title: Meniscus tears
d: A twist on the court or the job site, or a knee that slowly started catching and swelling. A torn meniscus is one of the most common knee problems, and many people get back to the things they enjoy with the right rehab.

title: Plantar fasciitis and heel pain
d: Sharp pain in the bottom of your heel with your first steps in the morning or after sitting. Hands-on therapy, stretching, taping, strengthening and footwear advice treat it without injections or surgery for most people.

title: Ankle sprains and Achilles pain
d: A rolled ankle that stays weak or keeps giving way, or Achilles pain that's worst with your first steps in the morning. Balance training after a sprain lowers the chance of another one, and progressive strengthening is the first treatment for Achilles pain.

title: Pulled muscles and muscle strains
d: A sudden grab in the hamstring, calf, groin or back mid-activity. Early gentle movement and progressive strengthening heal strains and help stop the same muscle going again.

title: Running injuries and running assessment
d: Knee pain a few miles in, shins that ache every time you add distance, a heel that hurts with the first steps of the day. Most running injuries can be treated without giving up running, and finding out why they happen is the key to keeping them away.

title: Youth sports injuries
d: A knee that aches after every practice, a heel that hurts in cleats, a throwing arm that won't settle down. Young athletes are still growing, and their injuries need care that fits a growing body and a safe plan to get back in the game.

title: Bladder leaks (urinary incontinence)
d: Leaking when you cough, sneeze, laugh, lift or exercise, or sudden urges you can't hold. Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is recommended as a first treatment for stress and mixed incontinence in women, before medication or surgery.

title: Accidental bowel leakage
d: Leaking gas or stool, or urgency you can't hold, often after childbirth or around menopause. Pelvic floor training and bowel habit changes are a recommended first treatment.

title: Pelvic organ prolapse
d: A feeling of heaviness, pressure or bulging in the vagina, often after childbirth or menopause and worse at the end of the day. Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is recommended for symptoms of mild to moderate prolapse, along with lifting and bowel habits that reduce strain.

title: Pelvic pain and painful sex
d: Pain with intercourse, pelvic or tailbone pain, or pain with tampons or exams is often linked to pelvic floor muscles that are tight or overworked. Pelvic floor therapy helps these muscles relax and work properly, gently and at your pace.

title: Interstitial cystitis and bladder pain
d: Bladder pain, pressure and frequent urges when tests keep coming back clear. Gentle pelvic floor therapy to relax tight muscles is recommended, rather than Kegels.

title: Diastasis recti (separated abdominal muscles)
d: A gap or bulge down the middle of your belly after pregnancy, sometimes with low back pain or a “pooch” that exercise hasn't fixed. Physical therapy retrains your deep core and pelvic floor to work together so you can return to exercise with confidence.

title: Back and pelvic pain during pregnancy
d: Pain in the low back, at the back of the pelvis or at the pubic bone, often worse turning in bed, on stairs or standing on one leg. Gentle, one-on-one prenatal physical therapy eases pain and keeps you moving, adjusted to each trimester.

title: C-section recovery
d: Scar tightness or numbness, a weak core, back pain, or trouble lifting your baby after a cesarean. Physical therapy helps you heal, rebuild your core and pelvic floor, and return to exercise.

title: Vertigo and dizziness (BPPV)
d: The room spins for a few seconds when you roll over in bed, lie down or look up. This is often BPPV, the most common cause of vertigo, and repositioning treatment by a trained physical therapist often helps within a few visits.

title: Balance problems and fall prevention
d: Feeling unsteady, holding onto furniture, or afraid of falling again. Balance can be trained at any age, and exercise programs that build balance and leg strength reduce falls in older adults.

title: TMJ and jaw pain
d: Aching in the jaw or temples, painful clicking, trouble opening wide, or clenching and grinding. Gentle hands-on care, jaw and neck exercises and habit changes are an effective first treatment for most TMJ problems.

title: Osteoporosis and bone health
d: If you've been told you have osteopenia or osteoporosis, the right exercise matters. Physical therapy teaches safe strengthening and weight-bearing exercise, balance training to lower your risk of falls, and ways to move that protect your spine.

title: Recovery after a broken bone
d: Stiff and weak after a cast, boot or fracture surgery. Rehab restores motion, strength and walking while following your doctor's instructions for the healing bone.

title: Getting stronger before surgery (prehab)
d: Building strength and motion before a planned knee, hip or shoulder surgery, learning the exercises you'll use afterward, and preparing your home and routine, so recovery starts on a better footing.

title: Knee and hip replacement rehab
d: Getting your new knee to bend and straighten, walking without a walker or limp, and handling stairs and the car again. One-on-one rehab that follows your surgeon's plan and precautions.

title: Rotator cuff repair and shoulder surgery rehab
d: Protecting the repair while it heals, then bringing back motion and strength, step by step with your surgeon's protocol.

title: Back and neck surgery rehab
d: After a discectomy, laminectomy or fusion: a walking plan, trunk and leg strength, and safe ways to bend and lift within your surgeon's precautions.

title: Recovery after surgery
d: Rehabilitation after joint replacement, ACL and rotator cuff repair, spine surgery and more, coordinated with your surgeon's protocol.
